new_statements.translation: [LLACAN] Language structure: notable features: retroflex vibrant affricate consonants; tone system (four registers). [Boyeldieu & Nougayrol 2008] The SBB languages have systems of two, three or four tone heights, whose correspondences follow specific formulas depending on whether nouns or verbs are considered. [...] The *SBB tone system is characterised by two distinctive tones. The western languages all derive from a later system (*OCC) which developed a third tone upwards. The appearance of a fourth level (extra-low) is late and limited (Yulu, Fer, Gula Koto).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Both quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators. (1) (and, the Internet Archive 20041122162226 of llacan.cnrs-bellevue.fr/francais/Rech/Langues/Fer.htm): "Structure de langue : traits remarquables : consonnes afriquées vibrantes rétroflexes; système tonal (quatre registres)." The page is a one-screen profile; it also gives autonym fɛ́r, region of Birao (northern CAR), ~4,000 speakers, classification SBB / Central Sudanic, and "la dénomination kara est courante mais impropre". No word on accent/stress. (2) (17 pp incl. HAL cover): extracted text of PDF pp.7-8 (= MS pp.6-7, page numbers printed at foot) reproduces exactly "Les langues SBB connaissent des systèmes à d…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Fer/Kara is a register-tone language with four contrastive tone levels (high, mid, low, extra-low); the accessible sources by its principal describer characterise its word prosody entirely in terms of lexical tone and make no statement about word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Both statements are about the lexical tone system of the language as a whole; neither says anything about word stress, phrase accent or citation forms. No accessible source addresses stress at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog kara1482 'Kara (Central African Republic)' = Fer (autonym fɛ́r), also 'Kara de Birao', Dam Fer, Fertit; ISO kah. LLACAN's page states 'la dénomination kara est courante mais impropre'. Santandrea 1970 describes 'Kara' of Bahr el Ghazal (Sudan), which Glottolog and WALS treat as the same language; Boyeldieu's 1989 'Yulu/Kara' title uses 'Kara' for Fer. Not to be confused with Yulu-Binga (yulu1243), whose Kara/Nguru dialect of Sudan LLACAN calls 'une variante dialectale du yulu'.

new_statements.quote: [p.46, §1.13] Le fer utilise à des fins distinctives la hauteur ou la modulation mélodiques qui contribuent ainsi à la définition d'une unité significative (...) tonal fonctionne sur la base de quatre registres (haut, moyen, bas et infra-bas) qui fondent l'identité de plusieurs unités tonales pertinentes, simples ou modulées (pour les monosyllabes), uniformes ou contrastées (pour les dissyllabes) [p.52] le schème tonal fonctionne plutôt comme un trait de l'unité significative (du "mot") que comme un trait de la voyelle ou de la syllabe
new_statements.translation: [p.46, §1.13] Fer makes distinctive use of pitch height or melodic modulation, which thus contribute to defining a meaningful unit (...) [the] tonal [system] operates on the basis of four registers (high, mid, low and extra-low) which underlie several relevant tonal units, level or contour (for monosyllables), uniform or contrasting (for disyllables). [p.52] the tone pattern functions rather as a feature of the meaningful unit (the 'word') than as a feature of the vowel or the syllable. (Also p.47, not in the quote: 'la pertinence semble bien se situer non pas au niveau du ton syllabique, mais à celui du schème tonal qui caractérise l'ensemble d'une unité significative' = relevance lies not at the level of syllabic tone but of the tone pattern of the whole meaningful unit.)

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (classification tonal; LLACAN Fer page 'système tonal (quatre registres)') and with the existing statement 'tone language, no stress statement': this is the primary description behind the LLACAN summary, and it names the four registers (haut, moyen, bas, infra-bas), places tonal distinctiveness at the level of the word's tone pattern, and - by whole-book full-text search - confirms that Boyeldieu 1987 makes no word-stress/accent statement for Fer (nor, by the same search, for Yulu). Nothing contradicts the catalog. Caveat on completeness: the tone and weak-syllable pages (46-54) were read through Gallica search snippets, not as full pages; a full-page read…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Fer is described as a tone language with four registers (H, M, L, extra-low); the distinctive unit is the tone pattern (schème tonal) of the whole word rather than the tone of a syllable; monosyllables carry level or contour patterns, disyllables uniform or contrasting ones. The book contains no statement about word stress or accent for Fer: the words accent/accentué/accentuation/accentuelle/proéminence/intonation do not occur anywhere in its scanned text, and 'intensité' occurs only for intervocalic consonant strengthening (p.43) and in a report of Caprile's 'contraste d'intensité syllabique' for Mbay and Palayer's analysis of Sar (p.52), i.e. for other Sara languages, cited while discussing Fer 'weak' syllables with a lax archiphonemic /a/.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (no stress statement at all).
new_statements.exceptions: Not stress rules but prosody-adjacent facts stated for Fer: §1.12 p.46 vowels of open-syllable monosyllables (V, CV) are markedly lengthened, independently of whether the tone is simple or modulated (n.7); p.51-54 final/'weak' syllables have lax vowel realisations that the author treats as non-phonemic supports of the last component of a contrasting tone pattern (a single archiphoneme /a/ in 'weak' syllable is considered); §1.16 p.50 uncertain extra-high realisations after a preceding High; p.50 R. Boyd's alternative three-register analysis (BiB as /MB/) is reported and rejected in favour of four functional registers.
new_statements.identity_note: The work's Fer sketch describes the fer ('kara') of Birao and surrounding villages, Vakaga prefecture, north-eastern Central African Republic (autonym fÈr; c. 3,500 speakers in 1981), from one speaker, Zakaria Sélémane of Toumo, recorded at Birao in November 1984 (p.37 §1.6); the author explicitly sets it apart from the 'Kara'/Yama of Sudan described by Santandrea 1970, 'dont la langue est sensiblement différente' (p.36 n.3). The second half of the book (pp.125-258) treats Yulu of Ouanda-Djallé (yulu1243), not read here beyond snippets.
